title: Live imaging of adult neural stem cells in freely behaving mice using mini-endoscopes
protocol: Prepare a mix of ice and water for animal anesthesia by hypothermia.
Install a glass pipette filled with mineral oil on an injector arm.
Cut the tip of the pipette, and lower the metal plunger of the injector to expel some oil from the pipette.
Lower the tip of the pipette into a 1-μL drop of DNA solution, and pull the metal plunger upward to draw the solution into the pipette.
Set the voltage of the electroporation generator for 100 volts with 5 square pulses, each pulse lasting 50 ms, and an interval of 950 ms between pulses.
Place one postnatal day 0–1 pup on ice for anesthesia.
Determine the state of anesthesia using the foot pinch response after approximately 5 minutes.
Proceed with an intraventricular injection of plasmids if no movement occurs upon foot pinching.
Place the pup in the stereotaxic apparatus, ensuring that the head is straight.
Sterilize the head with ethanol and chlorhexidine using cotton swabs.
Open the skin along the sagittal line of the skull by approximately 2 mm starting from the lambda.
Move the pipette anteriorly by 1.8 mm along the AP axis, zeroing on the sagittal suture.
Adjust the ML coordinate to move laterally by 0.8 mm (hemisphere of choice).
Zero dorso-ventral coordinates and lower the pipette slowly into the brain by 1.6 mm.
Inject the DNA solution.
Place electrodes coated with conductive gel on the surface of the bones, positive side on the lateral hemisphere where DNA was injected.
Initiate current transfer immediately after DNA injection using the pulse footswitch pedal.
Sweep the electrodes from dorsal to lateral sides at approximately 25° angle intervals for better area coverage.
Close the wound with forceps and apply Vetbond surgical glue.
Deeply anesthetize the animals using sodium pentobarbital (12 mg/mL; 0.1 mL per 10 g of body weight).
Perfuse the animals intracardially with 0.9% NaCl followed by 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA).
Collect the brains and post-fix them from 12 to 16 h at 4°C in 4% PFA.
Cut sagittal sections of the brains using a vibratome.
Perform isoflurane anesthesia (2%–3% isoflurane, oxygen flow at 1) by placing the animal in an induction chamber.
When the animal is anesthetized, shave the hair on the head.
Inject a local anesthetic and a non-inflammatory drug subcutaneously.
Place the animal on the stereotaxic setup under isoflurane anesthesia (1.5%–2%).
Remove any remaining hair on the head using depilatory cream.
Disinfect the surgical site.
Cut the skin on top of the head from between the ears to the anterior region of the eyes.
On each side of the initial cut, also cut out a small piece of skin in the region that will be surrounding the cannula once it is put in place.
Use four small clamps to pull aside the skin in front and in back of the cut to expose as much skull as possible.
Prepare a glass pipette using the same type used for electroporation.
Install the prepared pipette on an injector arm.
Cut the tip of the pipette to achieve an approximately 50–75-μm diameter tip.
Zero the coordinates at bregma.
Move to targeted implantation coordinates.
Drill a hole at the targeted coordinates using a medium tip burr.
Ensure the diameter of the drilled hole is about two times larger than the GRIN lens diameter.
Lower the glass pipette progressively into the brain tissue to prevent bleeding.
Clean the surface of the brain well using sterile saline solution and presoaked hemostatic sponges.
Remove the injector from the stereotaxic frame.
Install the fluorescence microscope holder to which the camera is attached.
Fix the GRIN lens cannula with the protrusion ring onto the microscope.
Turn on the microscope driver.
Launch the imaging software (Doric Neuroscience Studio).
Set microscope exposure time, gain, and LED efficiency to be able to visualize background fluorescence.
Start live imaging with the imaging software.
Ensure that the excitation light correctly exits the GRIN lens.
Clean the tip and sides of a previously used GRIN lens with water, soap, and 70% ethanol if necessary.
Position the GRIN lens above the hole drilled in the skull at the targeted XY coordinates.
Lower the GRIN lens to the bregma and set the XY coordinates to 0.
Center the excitation light spot on the bregma.
Draw an ROI on the acquired image using the imaging software.
Implant the GRIN lens in the brain.
Lower the GRIN lens into the brain using a relatively fast first push of approximately 100–200 μm to break into the tissue.
Wait approximately 3–5 min for the brain to stabilize.
Continue lowering the GRIN lens along the z axis in 50–100-μm increments.
Wait approximately 30 s to 1 min between each increment.
Track any significant change in background fluorescence levels when lowering the GRIN lens into the brain.
If the fluorescence intensity decreases, decrease the speed of insertion or increase the pause between increments.
If decreasing intensity occurs, remove the GRIN lens and begin lowering it again from the start.
If regular small increases in fluorescence occur at every increment, consider that the surface of GRIN is getting dirty or bleeding is occurring.
Remove the GRIN lens from the brain if regular increases are observed.
Clean the GRIN lens with 70% ethanol.
Lower the clean GRIN lens into the brain again.
Slow down the insertion of the GRIN lens as it approaches the targeted z depth.
Check for any increase in background fluorescence intensity on the fluorescence graph.
Stop lowering the implant when the protrusion ring starts to touch the skull.
If the distance between the spacer and the skull is too large (approximately 1 mm), remove the GRIN lens from the brain.
Change the protrusion ring for a thicker ring if needed.
Restart the implantation using the previously described steps (steps 15 to 21) if necessary.
If no significant change in background fluorescence is visible after lowering the GRIN lens, remove the GRIN lens from the brain.
Clean and reinstall the GRIN lens at slightly adjusted XY coordinates.
Fix the implanted GRIN lens cannula on the animal’s skull.
Fill the space between the skull and the protrusion ring with gel glue using a needle.
Avoid touching the camera and the place where the baseplate is attached to the camera while filling the space.
Focus particularly on areas with more space, especially if the GRIN lens cannula is installed at lateral coordinates.
Prepare Metabond dental cement by mixing 2 spoons of powder with 4 drops of solvent and 1 drop of catalyst according to manufacturer instructions.
Apply a first layer of dental cement using a disposable brush.
Avoid applying dental cement on the camera or where the baseplate is attached to the camera.
Prepare cement for a second layer by mixing two spoons of cement powder with 2–3 drops of solvent and 1 drop of catalyst.
Clean the brush with ethanol if you wish to reuse it.
Apply a third layer of cement, mixing half as much of every ingredient in order to fill any remaining empty spaces between the protrusion ring and the skull.
Sew the skin back together in front of and behind the implant.
Take caution when sewing near the animal’s eyes to avoid causing discomfort or injury.
Mix free space between the animal's skull and protrusion ring with glue gel using a bent needle where visible.
Apply dental cement all around the implant after the glue has dried.
Detach the microscope from the fixed cannula.
Habituate the mice to mini-endoscopic imaging by progressively increasing the time of consecutive imaging sessions from 1–2 hours to 24–48 hours.
Clean the lens of the camera as well as the top and sides of the implanted cannula with 70% ethanol or isopropyl alcohol using a cotton swab.
Dry the camera lens and the top of the cannula well using compressed air to remove residual dust or humidity.
Snap the mini-endoscope camera into the cannula baseplate using forceps to separate the lateral brackets.
Position the animal with the top of the head facing down while attaching the microscope on its baseplate to reduce pressure applied on the animal’s head and skull.
Transfer the animal to the imaging chamber.
Connect the wires (camera cable and optic fiber) to the mini-endoscope driver.
Launch Doric Studio imaging software.
Set the acquisition parameters (exposure time, gain, and LED efficiency) for one or both channels depending on the microscope used.
Launch live imaging to check for fluorescent labeling in the field of view.
Adapt the acquisition parameters if needed based on the fluorescent labeling quality.
If the labeling is satisfactory, launch acquisition.
Acquire images at a frame rate of 5–10 images every 15 minutes continuously for 2–3 days.
Average offline to obtain a single image from acquired frames.
Perform Ca2+ imaging of adult NSCs by acquiring 5–10 images every 30 seconds for 2–3 hours.
Optionally monitor animal activity in the arena during imaging.
Optionally evaluate naturalistic behaviors such as food and water intake by adding photobeams at food and water ports.
Use custom-made cages with photobeam-equipped food and water ports for monitoring behaviors.
Stop the imaging software at the end of the acquisition period.
Unplug the cables from the driver after stopping the imaging software.
Remove the animal from the arena after unplugging the cables.
Disconnect the camera from the GRIN lens cannula.
Place the animal back in its housing cage.
Perform isoflurane anesthesia by placing the animal in an induction chamber with 2%–3% isoflurane and oxygen flow at 1 L/min until anesthetized.
Place the anesthetized animal on a stereotaxic setup under isoflurane anesthesia (1.5%–2%, oxygen flow at 1 L/min).
Fix the dummy version of the microscope on the fluorescence microscope holder and install it on the stereotaxic frame.
Lower the microscope down the z-axis arm to snap it to the GRIN lens baseplate.
Drill the dental cement surrounding the baseplate using a medium tip burr.
Regularly remove dental cement dust with compressed air to maintain visibility around the implant.
Continue drilling until no residual resistance is experienced when pulling up the fluorescence microscope holder using the z-axis arm.
Ensure proper and complete drilling to remove the GRIN lens from the animal’s head to avoid damaging the brain.
For post-mortem analysis, stop isoflurane anesthesia and perfuse the animal as per steps 2 to 4 above to collect brains.
To reuse a GRIN lens for another experiment, carefully clean it by removing the spot of glue used during cannula preparation with a small blade.
Unscrew the protrusion ring from the implant baseplate.
Soak the implant for approximately 12 h in a mixture of distilled water and soap.
Carefully clean the implant using a cotton swab or Kimtech paper and 70% ethanol.
